originalStatement: Our commission has confirmed the suspension of several unregistered investment platforms found to be operating outside legal requirements.
headline: Regulators Really Do Publicly Suspend Unregistered Investment Platforms
articleBody:
This is true, and it describes routine, well documented regulatory work rather than anything unusual. Securities regulators, including the US Securities and Exchange Commission and equivalent bodies in other countries, regularly issue trading suspensions and enforcement actions against platforms operating without proper registration. These actions are published as official orders, with the platform named, the violation described, and the legal basis cited.

The pattern behind it is straightforward. Any platform letting people trade securities or crypto assets marketed as investments generally needs to register with the relevant regulator, a process built around disclosure requirements and investor protections. Platforms that skip registration avoid that oversight, which is precisely why regulators prioritize catching them. In recent enforcement cycles, regulators have specifically flagged a rise in unregistered online trading platforms.

The nuance is that "suspended" doesn't automatically mean "fraudulent." Some suspensions happen because a platform failed to file required paperwork rather than because it was actively scamming users, though both outcomes point to the same lesson: a platform's registration status is public information, and checking it before investing is a legitimate way to protect yourself.

sources.label: U.S. SEC, investor education resources on fraud and enforcement
Morgan Lewis, 'Securities Enforcement Roundup, April 2026'
Graphic Online, 'SEC sets deadline for all online investment platforms to register or face sanctions'

originalStatement: LEAKED: 80 percent of adults are secretly buried in payday loan debt right now and too embarrassed to tell anyone about it.
headline: No, 80 Percent of Adults Aren't Secretly Buried in Payday Loan Debt
articleBody:
The real numbers are nowhere close to this. According to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, about 4.7 percent of US households reported using a payday loan in a recent year, and roughly 12 million Americans use them annually, a small slice of the adult population, not four out of five people. Payday loan usage is also concentrated heavily among lower income households, with usage dropping off sharply as income rises.

The "leaked" and "too embarrassed to tell anyone" framing is doing a lot of work here. It's designed to make an outlandish number feel plausible by suggesting the real scale is hidden by shame rather than absent. But household debt, including payday lending, is tracked through public surveys and regulatory filings specifically because agencies need this data to write policy. A number this dramatic, four in five adults, would show up clearly in Federal Reserve household debt surveys and CFPB reports, and it simply doesn't.

None of this means payday loan debt isn't a real problem for the people who do use it. Borrowers who take one out often stay in a cycle of renewing or rolling over the loan for months, paying steep fees along the way. The issue with this claim isn't that payday debt is harmless. It's that the specific number attached to it was invented to sound shocking, not measured.

sources.label: National Debt Relief, payday loan usage data from Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
LendEDU, 'Payday Loan Statistics'

originalStatement: Half of all small businesses have supposedly shut down completely this year because of online marketplaces, according to a post going around.
headline: Small Businesses Aren't Being Wiped Out by Online Marketplaces at Anything Close to That Rate
articleBody:
This claim badly overstates both the scale and the cause of small business closures. Data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics and the Small Business Administration shows that around 20 to 22 percent of new US businesses close within their first year, and about half close within five years, but that is a cumulative figure spread across years of operation, not something that happens to half of all small businesses in a single year.

Online marketplace competition is a real pressure on some small businesses, particularly in retail categories where price competition is intense, but it's one factor among many. Surveys of business owners who actually closed point to a mix of causes: running out of cash, weak market demand, poor management, and general competition, of which online competition is only a part. Plenty of small businesses also use online marketplaces to their advantage, reaching customers well beyond their local area.

The core problem with a claim like this is that it takes a real, ongoing structural challenge and inflates it into a single shocking number with no attached source. Real business closure data comes from government statistical agencies and is published with clear methodology. A viral figure with no named source behind it isn't revealing a hidden crisis. It's a number built to spread, not to inform.

sources.label: LendingTree, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Business Employment Dynamics survival data
SCORE.org, 'Small Business Failure Rates in 2024: Summary'

originalStatement: The latest figures show the annual inflation rate holding at a relatively steady level compared to the previous reporting period.
headline: A Steady Inflation Reading Is a Verifiable Government Statistic, Not a Guess
articleBody:
This is true, and it's true in the most checkable way a claim can be: official inflation figures come from a national statistics agency on a fixed public schedule, calculated using a defined, published methodology. In the United States, that's the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which releases the Consumer Price Index monthly, always at the same time, always with the underlying data available for anyone to inspect. Other countries run equivalent offices with the same basic setup.

Recent US data shows exactly this kind of pattern in practice. Annual inflation eased to 3.5 percent in the twelve months through June 2026, down from 4.2 percent the month before, driven largely by falling energy prices after a period of elevated gas costs. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, also eased over the same stretch. Readings like these move around from month to month based on real economic forces, not the whims of whoever is reporting them.

The nuance to hold onto is that "steady" is relative and depends on the baseline you're comparing to. A rate holding steady compared to a recent spike looks very different from one holding steady at a chronically high level, so the full context, not just the headline word "steady," matters for understanding what it actually means for prices.

sources.label: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index news release
Trading Economics, 'United States Inflation Rate'

originalStatement: Official figures show tax revenue collection trending upward compared to the same period last year, according to our latest quarterly report.
headline: Official Tax Revenue Figures Are Public Record, and Checking Them Is Straightforward
articleBody:
This is true, and it holds up because government revenue collection is tracked and published with unusual transparency. In the United States, the Treasury Department releases a Monthly Treasury Statement covering receipts and outlays, and daily government revenue data is published through Treasury's own fiscal data platform. The Congressional Budget Office separately tracks and forecasts these numbers throughout the year. Anyone curious about whether revenue is really trending upward can look at the same figures the government itself uses.

Recent data shows this pattern holding in practice. The Congressional Budget Office's February 2026 baseline projected federal revenues would grow by roughly 6.9 percent for fiscal year 2026 compared with the prior year, and revenue collections through mid-2026 were tracking close to that projection, with individual income and payroll tax receipts running slightly ahead of expectations.

The nuance is that "trending upward" can mean different things depending on which revenue stream you're looking at. Individual income taxes, corporate taxes, tariffs, and payroll taxes don't always move in the same direction at the same time. A claim like this is easy to verify, but verifying it properly means checking the specific numbers behind the headline, not just taking "revenue is up" at face value.

sources.label: Congressional Budget Office, 'Revenue Collections Through the Individual Income Tax Filing Season'
U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, 'Government Revenue'
